fetched_contents.text: Azithromycin Resistance and Its Mechanism in Neisseria gonorrhoeae Strains in Hyogo, Japan Abstract Therapeutic options are limited for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection, especially for oral drugs. The purpose of this study was to investigate the susceptibility of N. gonorrhoeae to oral azithromycin (AZM) and the correlation between AZM resistance-related gene mutations and MIC. We examined the AZM MICs of clinical strains of N. gonorrhoeae, sequenced the peptidyltransferase loop in domain V of 23S rRNA, and investigated the statistical correlation between AZM MIC and the presence and number of the mutations. Among 59 N. gonorrhoeae strains, our statistical data showed that a deletion mutation was seen significantly more often in the higher-MIC group (0.5 μg/ml or higher) (35/37; 94.6%) than in the lower-MIC group (0.25 μg/ml or less) (4/22; 18.2%) (P < 0.0001). However, a mutation of codon 40 (Ala→Asp) in the mtrR gene (helix-turn-helix) was seen significantly more often in the lower-MIC group (12/22; 54.5%) (P < 0.0001). In N. gonorrhoeae multiantigen sequence typing (NG-MAST) analyses, ST4777 was representative of the lower-MIC group and ST1407, ST6798, and ST6800 were representative of the higher-MIC group. NG-MAST type 1407 was detected as the most prevalent type in AZM-resistant or -intermediate strains, as previously described. In conclusion, a deletion mutation in the mtrR promoter region may be a significant indicator for higher MIC (0.5 μg/ml or higher). ST4777 was often seen in the lower-MIC group, and ST1407, ST6798, and ST6800 were characteristic of the higher-MIC group. Further research with a greater number of strains would help elucidate the mechanism of AZM resistance in N. gonorrhoeae infection. INTRODUCTION Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection is often seen in male urethritis and female cervicitis, and its diagnosis has historically led to prompt initiation of treatments with a single antibiotic (1, 2). In the 1990s in most Asian countries, fluoroquinolones (FQs) were often used for this infection, partly because FQs have higher concentrations in the urinary tract. FQs showed good initial outcomes for this infection, but the results were not enduring. This may be partly due to the trend for single use of FQs for this infection, with no guidelines to recommend other choices (3–9). In addition to the FQs, cephalosporins such as cefixime were also recommended as oral antibiotics until these drugs showed decreased activity against N. gonorrhoeae (10). They are no longer a recommended choice for this infection (11–13). Oral antibiotics for outpatient treatment would be highly desirable for this kind of infection. Azithromycin (AZM) is an oral antibiotic with medical insurance approval for use against chlamydia infections (14), and there are many reports of good activity against N. gonorrhoeae infection (15). Other reports suggest that N. gonorrhoeae infection is less susceptible to AZM and that AZM-resistant strains have emerged (5). We investigated the AZM susceptibilities of N. gonorrhoeae strains and the correlation between mutations of macrolide resistance-related genes and the AZM MICs of clinically isolated strains of N. gonorrhoeae. Three mechanisms of resistance to AZM are known: overexpression of the efflux pump, mutation in the peptidyltransferase loop in domain V of 23S rRNA, and modification of the ribosomal target by methylase. Macrolides such as AZM and erythromycin (EM) bind to 4 alleles of the 23S rRNA component of the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome and restrain protein synthesis by inhibiting the elongation of peptide chains (16). Overexpression of the MtrCDE pump is due to either the lack of repressor MtrR protein, which occurs by a single-base-pair deletion or TT insertion in the promoter region, or missense mutations in the mtrR coding region (17). Modification of the ribosomal target by methylase or mutations reduces the affinity of the macrolide antibiotics for ribosomes (18). Since the use of antimicrobial agents for treatment of gonococcal infections is different in each country, the trend of drug resistance in gonococci is likely different geographically (19). Hence, epidemiological investigations should be done in each country. Previous studies have reported a high use of N. gonorrhoeae multiantigen sequence typing (NG-MAST), which is based on limited DNA sequence analyses of two highly polymorphic loci, porB and tbpB, in sequence type (ST) 1407 N. gonorrhoeae, which is multidrug resistant and appears to be disseminated basically worldwide (20). The selection and spread of AZM resistance are driven by inappropriate treatment of patients with suboptimal doses of AZM for gonococcal infection. N. gonorrhoeae maintains its genetic resistance determinants even after the removal of antibiotic selection pressure. Surveillance and characterization of the mechanisms of AZM resistance are essential. fetched_contents.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae 23S rRNA A2059G mutation is the only determinant necessary for high-level azithromycin resistance and improves in vivo biological fitness | Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy Abstract Objectives The global emergence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae isolates displaying high-level azithromycin resistance is a major concern for the currently recommended azithromycin/ceftriaxone dual therapy. N. gonorrhoeae high-level azithromycin resistance has been associated with an A2059G mutation in 23S rRNA. Here we investigated the specific contribution of this 23S rRNA A2059G mutation to high-level azithromycin resistance and its impact on biological fitness. Methods A2059G/G2059A alleles were specifically cloned into all four genomic copies of 23S rDNA of an azithromycin-susceptible isolate and a high-level azithromycin-resistant isolate. WT and mutant strains were subsequently investigated for azithromycin susceptibility using the agar dilution method. In addition, their biological fitness was studied by comparative liquid growth in the presence of hydrophobic and amphipathic compounds, by competition assays in a mouse vaginal tract infection model and by competition assays for invasion and intracellular survival. Results Azithromycin susceptibility analyses showed that the 23S rRNA A2059G mutation is the only genetic determinant required for N. gonorrhoeae to display the high-level azithromycin resistance phenotype. Further analysis of biological fitness showed that strains containing 2059G outcompeted isogenic strains containing 2059A for colonization in the mouse vaginal tract infection model and for invasion of HeLa cervical epithelial cells. Furthermore, the A2059G mutation enhanced growth in the presence of lithocholic acid or Triton X-100. Conclusions Our findings that the 23S rRNA A2059G mutation is sufficient for high-level azithromycin resistance and that this mutation generally enhanced the biological fitness of N. gonorrhoeae have important implications for the currently recommended treatment policies and antimicrobial stewardship programmes. fetched_contents.text: The novel 2024 WHO Neisseria gonorrhoeae reference strains for global quality assurance of laboratory investigations and superseded WHO N. gonorrhoeae reference strains—phenotypic, genetic and reference genome characterization Abstract Objectives MDR and XDR Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains remain major public health concerns internationally, and quality-assured global gonococcal antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance is imperative. The WHO global Gonococcal Antimicrobial Surveillance Programme (GASP) and WHO Enhanced GASP (EGASP), including metadata and WGS, are expanding internationally. We present the phenotypic, genetic and reference genome characteristics of the 2024 WHO gonococcal reference strains (n = 15) for quality assurance worldwide. All superseded WHO gonococcal reference strains (n = 14) were identically characterized. Material and Methods The 2024 WHO reference strains include 11 of the 2016 WHO reference strains, which were further characterized, and four novel strains. The superseded WHO reference strains include 11 WHO reference strains previously unpublished. All strains were characterized phenotypically and genomically (single-molecule PacBio or Oxford Nanopore and Illumina sequencing). Results The 2024 WHO reference strains represent all available susceptible and resistant phenotypes and genotypes for antimicrobials currently and previously used (n = 22), or considered for future use (n = 3) in gonorrhoea treatment. The novel WHO strains include internationally spreading ceftriaxone resistance, ceftriaxone resistance due to new penA mutations, ceftriaxone plus high-level azithromycin resistance and azithromycin resistance due to mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump. AMR, serogroup, prolyliminopeptidase, genetic AMR determinants, plasmid types, molecular epidemiological types and reference genome characteristics are presented for all strains. Conclusions The 2024 WHO gonococcal reference strains are recommended for internal and external quality assurance in laboratory examinations, especially in the WHO GASP, EGASP and other GASPs, but also in phenotypic and molecular diagnostics, AMR prediction, pharmacodynamics, epidemiology, research and as complete reference genomes in WGS analysis. Introduction Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Neisseria gonorrhoeae is compromising the treatment of gonorrhoea globally.1–8 Internationally, the extended-spectrum cephalosporin (ESC) ceftriaxone is the only remaining option for first-line empirical gonorrhoea therapy, i.e. given as a high-dose monotherapy or with azithromycin.1,2,8–18 However, gonococcal strains with resistance to ceftriaxone and especially azithromycin have been described globally.2,5–10 Furthermore, since 2015 international spread of the ceftriaxone-resistant MDR strain FC428 has been reported5,10,19–22 and since 2018 gonococcal XDR strains with ceftriaxone resistance combined with high-level azithromycin resistance have been described.23–27 Most of the currently identified ceftriaxone-resistant strains contain a mosaic penA-60.001 allele, which result in a mosaic penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2).5,10,19–28 The international spread of ceftriaxone-resistant MDR and XDR gonococcal strains and sporadic treatment failures with ceftriaxone (mainly of pharyngeal gonorrhoea) necessitate enhanced, quality-assured global gonococcal AMR surveillance.1–3,6–8 The WHO3 and ECDC29,30 have developed global and regional action plans, respectively, to control the transmission and impact of AMR gonococcal strains. One key component is to expand, improve and quality-assure the gonococcal AMR surveillance at local, national and global levels. The WHO global Gonococcal Antimicrobial Surveillance Programme (GASP) was relaunched in 2009 (www.who.int/initiatives/gonococcal-antimicrobial-surveillance-programme).3,6–8 Furthermore, the WHO Enhanced GASP (EGASP)26,31–33 is currently being expanded internationally (www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240021341). WHO EGASP includes isolate AMR data linked to patient metadata and WGS, which is already implemented in some regional GASPs.9,10 To fulfil all the aims of WHO GASP and EGASP, valid, internationally comparable and quality-assured AMR data are imperative. This is enabled through the use of WHO reference strains.34,35 In 2016, the latest WHO gonococcal reference strain panel was published.35 Herein, the 2024 WHO gonococcal reference strain panel is presented and characterized in detail. This panel includes 11 of the 2016 WHO reference strains (n = 14),35 which were further characterized, and four novel WHO reference strains. These novel WHO strains represent highly relevant AMR phenotypes and/or genotypes that were not available for inclusion in the previous WHO reference strain panels.34,35 The novel WHO strains include the internationally spreading ceftriaxone-resistant, mosaic penA-60.001-containing FC428 strain (associated with several ceftriaxone treatment failures),5,10,19–22 one strain expressing ceftriaxone resistance due to a new penA mutation (associated with cefixime treatment failure),36 the first cultured strain with ceftriaxone resistance plus high-level azithromycin resistance (mosaic penA-60.001-containing and with 23S rRNA gene A2059G mutations, associated with ceftriaxone 1 g plus doxycycline treatment failure)24 and one internationally spreading azithromycin-resistant strain with a mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump, i.e. with Neisseria lactamica-like mosaic 2 mtrR promoter and mtrD sequence.10,37,38 The 2024 WHO gonococcal reference strains were characterized in detail phenotypically {e.g. antibiograms [25 antimicrobials] and genetically [e.g. AMR determinants, multi-locus sequence typing (MLST),39,40N. gonorrhoeae multiantigen sequence typing (NG-MAST),40,41N. gonorrhoeae sequence typing for AMR (NG-STAR)42 and NG-STAR clonal complexes (CCs)43]}. Core genetic basis of azithromycin resistance in N. gonorrhoeae

The most commonly linked resistance mechanisms are 23S rRNA mutations and efflux pump-related changes, with the rRNA-targeted mutations being the most directly specific to azithromycin resistance. The 23S rRNA A2059G mutation is the central high-level resistance determinant, while the C2597T mutation in rrl is described as the most common mutation associated with medium-level azithromycin resistance (4–32 mg/L) [N1-R4]. In addition, multiple studies note that resistance can arise from mutations in the peptidyltransferase loop in domain V of the 23S rRNA gene [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-F2], and the WHO reference strain panel explicitly identifies the mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump and the 23S rRNA A2059G mutation as resistance-associated phenotypes [N5-F3].

How each mutation affects azithromycin binding or intracellular accumulation

Azithromycin binds to the 23S rRNA component of the bacterial ribosome, specifically to the peptidyltransferase loop in domain V, where it blocks protein synthesis by inhibiting elongation of the peptide chain [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The rRNA-targeted mutations reduce the affinity of the antibiotic for the ribosome, which is the direct mechanism of resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In contrast, efflux pump-related resistance works by increasing the removal of azithromycin from the bacterial cell rather than altering the target itself. The mtrR mutations and promoter-region changes that deregulate the MtrCDE efflux pump are associated with increased resistance because they reduce repression of the pump, allowing it to export azithromycin [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that efflux pump mutations can alter antibiotic binding or transport by changing the pump’s function or expression, though the exact mechanism is described less directly than for rRNA mutations [N6-R4][N6-R5].

Differences between rRNA-targeted and non-rRNA resistance mechanisms

The rRNA-targeted mechanism is the most specific and well-characterized for azithromycin resistance in N. gonorrhoeae. The A2059G mutation is described as the only genetic determinant required for high-level azithromycin resistance, and it is tied to a change in the ribosomal binding site that reduces antibiotic affinity [N2-F2]. The C2597T mutation is a separate rRNA variant associated with medium-level resistance [N1-R4]. Non-rRNA resistance mechanisms are broader and include efflux pump deregulation. The MtrCDE pump is the main efflux system implicated here, and mutations in mtrR or the mtrCDE promoter region increase resistance by derepressing the pump [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Another non-rRNA mechanism mentioned is the mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump, which is associated with azithromycin resistance in WHO reference strains [N5-F3]. This distinction matters because rRNA mutations alter the drug’s target, whereas efflux pump mutations alter its intracellular fate: the former reduces binding, while the latter increases export [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5].

Overall, the evidence suggests that azithromycin resistance in N. gonorrhoeae is genetically heterogeneous but dominated by 23S rRNA mutations, especially A2059G, and by efflux pump deregulation, especially the MtrCDE system. The rRNA mutations are the most specific and directly mechanistic, whereas efflux pump changes represent a broader, secondary class of resistance [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N8:
Evidence for mutation-specific resistance magnitude and clinical relevance

How MICs vary with different mutations or combinations

The evidence shows that the same mutation can produce different MIC ranges depending on the strain and the study. The study in Hyogo, Japan, found that a deletion mutation in the mtrR promoter region was significantly more common in higher-MIC groups (0.5 μg/ml or higher), while the mtrR codon 40 mutation was more common in lower-MIC groups [N1-F1]. The WHO reference strain panel reports that the mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump is associated with azithromycin resistance, and the 23S rRNA A2059G mutation is associated with high-level azithromycin resistance [N5-F3]. A separate study notes that the A2059G mutation is the only determinant required for high-level azithromycin resistance, while the C2597T mutation is linked to medium-level resistance (4–32 mg/L) [N1-R4][N2-F2]. These findings indicate that mutations can span a broad resistance spectrum: high-level, medium-level, and lower-level resistance, depending on the mutation and the number of copies or the efflux background [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Which mutations are most predictive of clinical resistance

The most predictive mutations appear to be the 23S rRNA A2059G mutation for high-level resistance and the mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump for broader resistance-associated phenotypes [N2-F2][N5-F3]. The Hyogo study also suggests that the mtrR promoter deletion is strongly associated with higher MICs, and the mtrR codon 40 mutation with lower MICs [N1-F1]. These results imply that clinical resistance is not captured by a single mutation alone but depends on the combination of mutations and the background genotype. The WHO reference strains emphasize that the mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump and the 23S rRNA A2059G mutation are clinically meaningful resistance phenotypes [N5-F3].

Limitations and uncertainty in associating mutations with resistance

The evidence is not fully definitive because the associations are often statistical or epidemiological rather than absolute. The Hyogo study found significant differences in mutation prevalence by MIC group but also noted that further research with a greater number of strains would help clarify the mechanism [N1-F1]. The WHO reference strains note that resistance patterns can vary across settings and that surveillance is needed to capture the full spectrum of AMR determinants [N5-F3]. The evidence also highlights that resistance can be influenced by multiple factors, including efflux pump status, plasmid content, and other AMR determinants, so a mutation alone may not fully explain the MIC or clinical outcome [N5-F3]. In short, the strongest associations are between A2059G and high-level resistance, C2597T and medium-level resistance, and MtrCDE deregulation and broader resistance, but the relationship remains context-dependent and not fully mechanistically universal [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N9:
Surveillance context and implications for resistance interpretation

Prevalence of resistance-associated mutations in surveillance data

Surveillance data indicate that azithromycin resistance-associated mutations are not rare, but their prevalence varies by setting and over time. The WHO reference strain panel explicitly states that the 2024 strains represent all available susceptible and resistant phenotypes and genotypes for current and previously used antimicrobials, including azithromycin resistance due to mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump and the 23S rRNA A2059G mutation [N5-F3]. The Hyogo study also found that a deletion mutation in the mtrR promoter was highly prevalent in higher-MIC groups, whereas the mtrR codon 40 mutation was more common in lower-MIC groups [N1-F1]. These findings suggest that surveillance should include both rRNA and efflux pump markers, because resistance determinants can differ by region and by strain lineage [N5-F3][N1-F1].

How resistance patterns have changed over time

The evidence suggests that azithromycin resistance is increasing and becoming more complex. The WHO reference strains include strains with ceftriaxone plus high-level azithromycin resistance and mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump resistance, reflecting the emergence of combined resistance phenotypes [N5-F3]. The WHO fact sheet and surveillance context also note that WHO GASP and EGASP are expanding globally to better capture AMR trends, indicating that resistance interpretation is increasingly dependent on standardized surveillance [N5-R1][N5-F3]. The reference strains further show that resistance can be driven by both chromosomal and plasmid-related changes, and that resistance determinants can spread internationally [N5-F3]. Taken together, the surveillance evidence implies that azithromycin resistance is no longer a simple single-mutation problem; it is now more likely to be part of broader resistance networks [N5-R1][N5-F3].

Clinical and public health implications of mutation detection

Mutation detection has important clinical and public health implications. First, it can help identify resistant strains and guide treatment decisions. The WHO reference strains are recommended for quality assurance in laboratory investigations, and they include resistance-associated phenotypes that are relevant to treatment failure [N5-F3]. Second, mutation detection supports surveillance and outbreak investigation. The WHO notes that quality-assured global AMR surveillance is imperative, and that reference strains are used to standardize data across laboratories [N5-R1][N5-F3]. Third, mutation detection can reveal resistance mechanisms and help monitor resistance emergence. The Hyogo study used mutation detection to correlate MICs with resistance-associated genes and to identify ST types associated with different MIC ranges [N1-F1]. Finally, the evidence underscores that mutation detection should be interpreted cautiously, because resistance can be influenced by multiple factors, including efflux pump status and other AMR determinants [N5-F3]. Overall, mutation detection is a useful but incomplete tool: it can signal resistance, but it must be combined with MIC testing and contextual surveillance data to interpret resistance accurately [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Non-23S rRNA resistance mechanisms and efflux pump biology

Which efflux components or regulators are associated with resistance

The main efflux system implicated in azithromycin resistance is the MtrCDE multidrug efflux pump. The evidence repeatedly associates mutations in mtrR and the mtrCDE promoter region with increased azithromycin resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The WHO reference strains also specifically include a mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump as an azithromycin resistance-associated phenotype [N5-F3]. In addition, the evidence points to interspecific acquisition of an efflux pump component and a transcriptional regulator as a mechanism of azithromycin resistance, indicating that resistance can be acquired from other Neisseria species [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This suggests that the MtrCDE system is central, but that its regulation and components can be altered by both chromosomal and horizontally acquired changes [N4-R1][N4-R2].

How efflux pump mutations alter antibiotic binding or transport

The evidence indicates that efflux pump mutations primarily alter transport rather than binding. The mtrR mutations and promoter-region changes deregulate the MtrCDE pump, reducing repression and increasing pump expression or activity [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. This allows the pump to export azithromycin more efficiently, thereby reducing intracellular accumulation and resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that efflux pump antibiotic-binding-site mutations are associated with azithromycin nonsusceptibility in clinical isolates [N4-R3][N4-R5], suggesting that some efflux mutations may also alter the pump’s interaction with the antibiotic. Taken together, the mechanism is best described as deregulation of export plus, in some cases, altered binding-site function [N4-R3][N4-R5].

How these mechanisms differ from rRNA-mediated resistance

The rRNA-mediated mechanisms act at the target level: azithromycin binds to the 23S rRNA, and mutations in that region reduce binding affinity, leading to resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2]. In contrast, efflux pump mechanisms act at the cell surface: they increase the removal of azithromycin from the bacterial cell, so the drug is less likely to reach a concentration sufficient to inhibit protein synthesis [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The key difference is therefore one of localization and mechanism: rRNA mutations alter the drug’s target, whereas efflux pump mutations alter its intracellular fate [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The WHO reference strains also emphasize that mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump resistance is a separate clinical phenotype from the 23S rRNA A2059G mutation, further highlighting that these are distinct resistance pathways [N5-F3]. So, while both mechanisms contribute to resistance, they do so through different biological processes and should be interpreted as separate but sometimes interacting resistance determinants [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N11:
Integrated explanation of how specific genetic mutations contribute to varying azithromycin resistance

## 1) The main genetic mechanisms driving azithromycin resistance

The evidence shows that resistance to azithromycin in *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* arises from two main classes of genetic changes: **rRNA-targeted mutations** and **non-rRNA resistance mechanisms, especially efflux pump deregulation** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, and their relative contribution can vary across strains and settings.

### A) rRNA-targeted mutations

The most specific and well-characterized resistance mechanism is a mutation in the **23S rRNA gene**. The **A2059G mutation** is described as the **only genetic determinant required for high-level azithromycin resistance** [N2-F2]. It is also strongly associated with high-level resistance in WHO reference strains [N5-F3]. In addition, the **C2597T mutation in rrl** is reported as the **most common mutation associated with medium-level azithromycin resistance (4–32 mg/L)** [N1-R4]. Other studies note that resistance can arise from **mutations in the peptidyltransferase loop in domain V of the 23S rRNA gene** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R2]. These mutations reduce the affinity of azithromycin for its ribosomal target, which is the direct mechanism of resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### B) Non-rRNA resistance mechanisms

Non-rRNA resistance is dominated by **efflux pump deregulation**, particularly the **MtrCDE multidrug efflux pump**. Mutations in **mtrR** or the **mtrCDE promoter region** reduce repression of the pump, leading to increased expression or activity and thus greater resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The WHO reference strains explicitly identify a **mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump** as an azithromycin resistance-associated phenotype [N5-F3]. This means that resistance can be driven not only by the ribosome itself, but also by the bacterium’s ability to actively remove the drug.

The evidence also points to **interspecific acquisition** of efflux pump components and regulators as a source of resistance [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This adds complexity because it shows that resistance can be acquired from other *Neisseria* species rather than arising only from chromosomal mutations.

## 2) How specific mutations affect azithromycin binding or intracellular accumulation

### rRNA-targeted mutations: altering the drug’s target

Azithromycin binds to the **23S rRNA component of the 50S ribosomal subunit**, specifically to the **peptidyltransferase loop in domain V**, where it blocks protein synthesis by inhibiting elongation of the peptide chain [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The rRNA mutations reduce the affinity of the antibiotic for the ribosome, which means the drug is less effective at inhibiting the target [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The A2059G mutation is especially important for **high-level resistance**, while C2597T is associated with **medium-level resistance** [N1-R4][N2-F2].

### efflux pump-related mutations: altering the intracellular fate of the drug

Efflux pump mutations do not alter the ribosome itself, but they increase the removal of azithromycin from the bacterial cell. The **MtrCDE efflux pump** is the main efflux system implicated here, and mutations in **mtrR** or the **mtrCDE promoter region** derepress the pump, increasing its activity and allowing more drug to be exported [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that efflux pump antibiotic-binding-site mutations are associated with azithromycin nonsusceptibility in clinical isolates [N4-R3][N4-R5], suggesting that some efflux changes may also alter the pump’s interaction with the antibiotic. Overall, these mutations reduce intracellular accumulation rather than directly altering the target [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 3) How these mechanisms differ from one another

The key distinction is whether the mutation acts at the **drug-target level** or at the **cell-surface transport level**. 

- **rRNA-targeted resistance** changes the way azithromycin binds to its ribosomal target, reducing its effectiveness at inhibiting protein synthesis [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Non-rRNA resistance, especially efflux pump resistance**, changes the way the drug is handled inside the cell. It increases export and lowers intracellular concentration, so the drug is less likely to reach a concentration sufficient to inhibit the target [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 4) Mutation-specific resistance magnitude and clinical relevance

### How MICs vary with different mutations or combinations

The evidence shows that the same mutation can produce very different MIC ranges depending on the strain and the background genotype. - **A2059G** for **high-level resistance** [N2-F2],
- **C2597T** for **medium-level resistance** [N1-R4],
- and **MtrCDE deregulation** for broader resistance-associated phenotypes [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].

These are not absolute predictors in every setting, but they are the strongest associations supported by the evidence. The WHO reference strains emphasize that these resistance determinants are clinically meaningful and are included in global surveillance panels [N5-F3].

There are important limitations to interpreting mutations as direct causes of resistance. First, the evidence is often **statistical or epidemiological** rather than definitive. Surveillance data show that azithromycin resistance-associated mutations are not rare, but their prevalence varies by region and over time. Mutation detection has important practical implications:

Specific genetic mutations in *N. gonorrhoeae* contribute to varying azithromycin resistance in a genetically heterogeneous way. The main mechanisms are:

- **rRNA-targeted mutations**, especially **A2059G**, which reduce ribosomal binding and are most specific to high-level resistance [N2-F2][N5-F3],
- **efflux pump deregulation**, especially the **MtrCDE system**, which increases drug export and can contribute to broader resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3],

The evidence shows that resistance to azithromycin in *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* arises from two main classes of genetic changes: **rRNA-targeted mutations** and **non-rRNA resistance mechanisms, especially efflux pump deregulation** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The most specific and well-characterized resistance mechanism is a mutation in the **23S rRNA gene**. It is also strongly associated with high-level resistance in WHO reference strains [N5-F3]. In addition, the **C2597T mutation in rrl** is reported as the **most common mutation associated with medium-level azithromycin resistance (4–32 mg/L)** [N1-R4]. Other studies note that resistance can arise from **mutations in the peptidyltransferase loop in domain V of the 23S rRNA gene** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R2]. These mutations reduce the affinity of azithromycin for its ribosomal target, which is the direct mechanism of resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### B) Non-rRNA resistance mechanisms

Non-rRNA resistance is dominated by **efflux pump deregulation**, particularly the **MtrCDE multidrug efflux pump**. Mutations in **mtrR** or the **mtrCDE promoter region** reduce repression of the pump, leading to increased expression or activity and thus greater resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The WHO reference strains explicitly identify a **mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump** as an azithromycin resistance-associated phenotype [N5-F3]. This means that resistance can be driven not only by the ribosome itself, but also by the bacterium’s ability to actively remove the drug.

The evidence also points to **interspecific acquisition** of efflux pump components and regulators as a source of resistance [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This adds complexity because it shows that resistance can be acquired from other *Neisseria* species rather than arising only from chromosomal mutations.

### rRNA-targeted mutations: altering the drug’s target

Azithromycin binds to the **23S rRNA component of the 50S ribosomal subunit**, specifically to the **peptidyltransferase loop in domain V**, where it blocks protein synthesis by inhibiting elongation of the peptide chain [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Efflux pump mutations do not alter the ribosome itself, but they increase the removal of azithromycin from the bacterial cell. The **MtrCDE efflux pump** is the main efflux system implicated here, and mutations in **mtrR** or the **mtrCDE promoter region** derepress the pump, increasing its activity and allowing more drug to be exported [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence also notes that efflux pump antibiotic-binding-site mutations are associated with azithromycin nonsusceptibility in clinical isolates [N4-R3][N4-R5], suggesting that some efflux changes may also alter the pump’s interaction with the antibiotic. Overall, these mutations reduce intracellular accumulation rather than directly altering the target [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 3) How these mechanisms differ from one another

The key distinction is whether the mutation acts at the **drug-target level** or at the **cell-surface transport level**. 

- **rRNA-targeted resistance** changes the way azithromycin binds to its ribosomal target, reducing its effectiveness at inhibiting protein synthesis [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Non-rRNA resistance, especially efflux pump resistance**, changes the way the drug is handled inside the cell. It increases export and lowers intracellular concentration, so the drug is less likely to reach a concentration sufficient to inhibit the target [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

The WHO reference strains emphasize that these are **distinct resistance pathways**: the **23S rRNA A2059G mutation** is one phenotype, while the **mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump** is a separate phenotype [N5-F3]. This matters because a single mutation does not capture the full picture of resistance. Some strains may carry both a ribosomal mutation and an efflux pump change, and the combined effect can be greater than either alone [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].

## 4) Mutation-specific resistance magnitude and clinical relevance

### How MICs vary with different mutations or combinations

The evidence shows that the same mutation can produce very different MIC ranges depending on the strain and the background genotype. The Hyogo, Japan study found that a **deletion mutation in the mtrR promoter region** was significantly more common in higher-MIC groups (0.5 μg/ml or higher), while the **mtrR codon 40 mutation** was more common in lower-MIC groups [N1-F1]. This indicates that mutation-associated MICs are not uniform and can depend on promoter context and efflux background.

The WHO reference strains also show that the **23S rRNA A2059G mutation** is associated with **high-level azithromycin resistance**, while the **C2597T mutation** is associated with **medium-level resistance** [N1-R4][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump is associated with broader resistance-associated phenotypes [N5-F3]. These findings suggest that azithromycin resistance can span a wide spectrum: from low-level to high-level resistance, depending on the combination of mutations and the overall genetic background [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].

### Which mutations are most predictive of clinical resistance

The most predictive mutations appear to be:

- **A2059G** for **high-level resistance** [N2-F2],
- **C2597T** for **medium-level resistance** [N1-R4],
- and **MtrCDE deregulation** for broader resistance-associated phenotypes [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].

These are not absolute predictors in every setting, but they are the strongest associations supported by the evidence. The WHO reference strains emphasize that these resistance determinants are clinically meaningful and are included in global surveillance panels [N5-F3].

### Limitations and uncertainty in associating mutations with resistance

There are important limitations to interpreting mutations as direct causes of resistance. First, the evidence is often **statistical or epidemiological** rather than definitive. The Hyogo study found significant associations but noted that more strains would be needed to fully clarify the mechanism [N1-F1]. Second, resistance can be influenced by multiple factors, including efflux pump status, other AMR determinants, and the broader genomic background [N5-F3]. Third, mutation detection alone may not fully explain the MIC or clinical outcome [N5-F3].

Because of these uncertainties, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: while certain mutations are strongly associated with resistance, they should be used in combination with MIC testing and surveillance data to make the best clinical and public health decisions [N1-F1][N5-F3].

## 5) Surveillance context and implications for resistance interpretation

### Prevalence of resistance-associated mutations in surveillance data

Surveillance data show that azithromycin resistance-associated mutations are not rare, but their prevalence varies by region and over time. The WHO reference strains include strains representing **all available susceptible and resistant phenotypes** for current and previously used antimicrobials, including the **23S rRNA A2059G mutation** and the **mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump** [N5-F3]. The Hyogo study also found that a **deletion mutation in the mtrR promoter region** was highly prevalent in higher-MIC groups, whereas the **mtrR codon 40 mutation** was more common in lower-MIC groups [N1-F1]. These findings suggest that surveillance should include both rRNA and efflux pump markers, because resistance determinants can differ by lineage and setting [N5-F3][N1-F1].

### How resistance patterns have changed over time

The evidence suggests that azithromycin resistance is becoming more complex and widespread. The WHO reference strains include strains with **ceftriaxone plus high-level azithromycin resistance** and **mosaic MtrRCDE efflux pump resistance**, reflecting the emergence of combined resistance phenotypes [N5-F3]. The WHO surveillance context also notes that global quality-assured AMR surveillance is expanding, indicating that resistance interpretation is increasingly dependent on standardized surveillance systems [N5-R1][N5-F3]. This means that resistance patterns are not static and are shaped by both local and global epidemiology [N5-R1][N5-F3].

### Clinical and public health implications of mutation detection

Mutation detection has important practical implications:

1. It can help identify resistant strains and guide treatment decisions [N5-F3].
2. It supports surveillance and outbreak investigation by standardizing resistance markers [N5-R1][N5-F3].
3. It can reveal resistance mechanisms and help monitor resistance emergence [N1-F1][N5-F3].
4. It can reveal the spread of resistance determinants, including those acquired from other *Neisseria* species [N4-R1][N4-R2].

However, mutation detection should be interpreted cautiously. Resistance is often multifactorial, and a single mutation may not fully explain the MIC or clinical outcome [N5-F3]. Because of this, mutation detection should be combined with MIC testing and contextual surveillance data to interpret resistance accurately [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-F3].

## 6) Bottom line

Specific genetic mutations in *N. gonorrhoeae* contribute to varying azithromycin resistance in a genetically heterogeneous way. The main mechanisms are:

- **rRNA-targeted mutations**, especially **A2059G**, which reduce ribosomal binding and are most specific to high-level resistance [N2-F2][N5-F3],
- **efflux pump deregulation**, especially the **MtrCDE system**, which increases drug export and can contribute to broader resistance [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3],
- and **interspecific acquisition** of efflux pump components and regulators, which expands the range of possible resistance pathways [N4-R1][N4-R2].

The same mutation can produce different MICs depending on the strain background, and the strongest associations are not universal. Therefore, mutation detection is a useful but incomplete tool: it should be interpreted alongside MIC data and surveillance context to understand whether resistance is likely and how it should be managed [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3].
